**The Catiline Conspiracy and the Roman Senate's Response**

**Early plot of the conspiracy.** According to Sallust, Catiline and Autronius, in concert with Piso, planned to assassinate the consuls Lucius Cotta and Lucius Torquatus in the Capitol on the first of January, at which point—having seized the fasces (the consular authority)—they intended to send Piso with an army to seize the two Spains. This design was discovered, however, and the assassination was postponed.

**The attempted coup before the senate-house.** Sallust also records that a strike was planned at the senate-house itself: had Catiline, who was standing in front of the senate-house, not given the signal to his associates too hastily, "there would that day have been perpetrated the most atrocious outrage since the city of Rome was founded." But the armed conspirators had not assembled in sufficient numbers, and the want of force frustrated the design.

**Threat to the consul Cicero.** Cassius Dio describes how the conspiracy's leader "set forth in detail how great punishments they would suffer if they were detected and how many desirable things they would obtain if successful, and by such means encouraged and incited them, that two men promised to rush into Cicero's house at daybreak and murder him there." Dio adds that information of this plot was given in advance—Cicero, being informed, was forewarned. The conspiracy was thus uncovered while it was in progress.

**The Senate's deliberation and division.** The Senate's response, as recorded by Suetonius, turned on the fate of the arrested accomplices. "After he was chosen praetor, the conspiracy of Catiline was discovered; and while every other member of the senate voted for inflicting capital punishment on the accomplices in that crime, he [Julius Caesar] alone proposed that the delinquents should be distributed for safe custody among the towns of Italy, their property being confiscated." In other words, the overwhelming majority of senators voted for the execution of the detained conspirators, while Caesar alone dissented, arguing for their distribution and safe custody in Italian towns rather than capital punishment.

**The aftermath and Cicero's prestige.** Plutarch records that the conspiracy's exposure made the consul Cicero's authority very great in the city, though he also created much envy by repeatedly lauding himself—so much so that no meeting of the senate, the people's assembly, or the courts could occur without his bringing up Catiline and Lentulus (the latter being one of the leading arrested conspirators). Plutarch further notes that the people so extolled Cicero's consulate that the greatest honors were decreed to him, and he was publicly declared "the Father of his Country"—a title Suetonius likewise confirms was first conferred on Cicero ("Cicero was the first who received the honour of being called 'Pater patriae'"), with Plutarch specifying that the title was given when Cato conferred it upon him in an address to the people.

**Summary.** The evidence presents the Catiline conspiracy as a planned violent seizure of power that involved both an attempted assassination of the consuls in the Capitol and a strike near the senate-house, as well as a plot to murder the consul Cicero in his home. The conspiracy was discovered in advance, the leading accomplices were arrested, and the Senate, meeting on the conspirators' fate, voted overwhelmingly for their capital punishment, with only Julius Caesar proposing the milder alternative of detention in Italian towns and confiscation of property. The successful suppression of the conspiracy brought great honor to Cicero, who was honored with the unprecedented title of "Father of his Country."

**Evidence limitations.** The retrieved sources date and sequence some events only partially: the historical events record includes an assassination plot (Lucius Cotta and Lucius Torquatus) whose temporal grounding is marked as unresolved, and several excerpts lack precise section locators. The sources also do not supply the specific date on which the Senate voted on the conspirators' punishment, nor the names of most of the accomplices beyond Lentulus and the leaders Catiline and Autronius. Caesar's minority position is the only dissenting motion explicitly preserved in the evidence; the names of the senators who formed the majority are not given. historical_evidence.text: After he was chosen praetor, the conspiracy of Catiline was discovered; and while every other member of the senate voted for inflicting capital punishment on the accomplices in that crime [33], he alone proposed that the delinquents should be distributed for safe custody among the towns of Italy, their property being confiscated. He even struck such terror into those who were advocates for greater severity, by representing to them what universal odium would be attached to their memories by the Roman people, that Decius Silanus, consul elect, did not hesitate to qualify his proposal, it not being very honourable to change it, by a lenient interpretation; as if it had been understood in a harsher sense than he intended, and Caesar would certainly have carried his point, having brought over to his side a great number of the senators, among whom was Cicero, the consul's brother, had not a speech by Marcus Cato infused new vigour into the resolutions of the senate.

state.final_answer:
**The Catiline Conspiracy and the Roman Senate's Response**

**Early plot of the conspiracy.** According to Sallust, Catiline and Autronius, in concert with Piso, planned to assassinate the consuls Lucius Cotta and Lucius Torquatus in the Capitol on the first of January, at which point—having seized the fasces (the consular authority)—they intended to send Piso with an army to seize the two Spains. This design was discovered, however, and the assassination was postponed.

**The attempted coup before the senate-house.** Sallust also records that a strike was planned at the senate-house itself: had Catiline, who was standing in front of the senate-house, not given the signal to his associates too hastily, "there would that day have been perpetrated the most atrocious outrage since the city of Rome was founded." But the armed conspirators had not assembled in sufficient numbers, and the want of force frustrated the design.

**Threat to the consul Cicero.** Cassius Dio describes how the conspiracy's leader "set forth in detail how great punishments they would suffer if they were detected and how many desirable things they would obtain if successful, and by such means encouraged and incited them, that two men promised to rush into Cicero's house at daybreak and murder him there." Dio adds that information of this plot was given in advance—Cicero, being informed, was forewarned. The conspiracy was thus uncovered while it was in progress.

**The Senate's deliberation and division.** The Senate's response, as recorded by Suetonius, turned on the fate of the arrested accomplices. "After he was chosen praetor, the conspiracy of Catiline was discovered; and while every other member of the senate voted for inflicting capital punishment on the accomplices in that crime, he [Julius Caesar] alone proposed that the delinquents should be distributed for safe custody among the towns of Italy, their property being confiscated." In other words, the overwhelming majority of senators voted for the execution of the detained conspirators, while Caesar alone dissented, arguing for their distribution and safe custody in Italian towns rather than capital punishment.

**The aftermath and Cicero's prestige.** Plutarch records that the conspiracy's exposure made the consul Cicero's authority very great in the city, though he also created much envy by repeatedly lauding himself—so much so that no meeting of the senate, the people's assembly, or the courts could occur without his bringing up Catiline and Lentulus (the latter being one of the leading arrested conspirators). Plutarch further notes that the people so extolled Cicero's consulate that the greatest honors were decreed to him, and he was publicly declared "the Father of his Country"—a title Suetonius likewise confirms was first conferred on Cicero ("Cicero was the first who received the honour of being called 'Pater patriae'"), with Plutarch specifying that the title was given when Cato conferred it upon him in an address to the people.

**Summary.** The evidence presents the Catiline conspiracy as a planned violent seizure of power that involved both an attempted assassination of the consuls in the Capitol and a strike near the senate-house, as well as a plot to murder the consul Cicero in his home. The conspiracy was discovered in advance, the leading accomplices were arrested, and the Senate, meeting on the conspirators' fate, voted overwhelmingly for their capital punishment, with only Julius Caesar proposing the milder alternative of detention in Italian towns and confiscation of property. The successful suppression of the conspiracy brought great honor to Cicero, who was honored with the unprecedented title of "Father of his Country."

**Evidence limitations.** The retrieved sources date and sequence some events only partially: the historical events record includes an assassination plot (Lucius Cotta and Lucius Torquatus) whose temporal grounding is marked as unresolved, and several excerpts lack precise section locators. The sources also do not supply the specific date on which the Senate voted on the conspirators' punishment, nor the names of most of the accomplices beyond Lentulus and the leaders Catiline and Autronius. Caesar's minority position is the only dissenting motion explicitly preserved in the evidence; the names of the senators who formed the majority are not given.
